### Internal Instruments in Dynamic Panels {#sec-dynamic-panel-iv}

Every instrument family so far has imported variation from outside the model: a judge, a shock,
a distance, an airline route. Dynamic panel GMM does something different. It builds instruments
out of the dependent variable's own history, which is why it is so heavily used in finance,
strategy, and management, where a credible external instrument for leverage, board structure, or
diversification is rarely on offer and a long firm-year panel usually is.

The construction is elegant and the estimator is easy to run, which is precisely the problem.
This section shows what it identifies, and then shows how much the answer moves on choices that
look like implementation details.

#### Why Least Squares and Fixed Effects Both Fail

Consider the workhorse specification

$$
y_{it} = \rho\, y_{i,t-1} + x_{it}'\beta + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it},
$$

with a firm effect $\alpha_i$ that is correlated with the regressors. Two familiar estimators
both break, and they break in opposite directions.

Pooled least squares omits $\alpha_i$, which is part of $y_{i,t-1}$ by construction, so the
lagged dependent variable picks up the firm effect and $\hat\rho$ is biased upward. The within
transformation removes $\alpha_i$, but demeaning makes the transformed lag correlated with the
transformed error, because $\bar{y}_{i}$ contains $\varepsilon_{it}$. @nickell1981biases showed
this bias is of order $1/T$ and is downward. In the short panels typical of firm data it is
large.

So the two default estimators bracket the truth, which is a useful diagnostic and a terrible
estimator.

```{r dynpanel-nickell, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(plm)
set.seed(7)

sim <- function(N = 200, Tt = 6, rho = 0.6) {
  a <- rnorm(N)                                   # firm effects
  y <- matrix(0, N, Tt + 50)
  y[, 1] <- a / (1 - rho) + rnorm(N)
  for (t in 2:(Tt + 50)) y[, t] <- rho * y[, t - 1] + a + rnorm(N)
  y <- y[, (50 + 1):(50 + Tt)]                    # discard the burn-in
  p <- pdata.frame(data.frame(id = rep(1:N, each = Tt), t = rep(1:Tt, N),
                              y = as.vector(t(y))), index = c("id", "t"))
  c(pooled = unname(coef(plm(y ~ lag(y), data = p, model = "pooling"))[2]),
    within = unname(coef(plm(y ~ lag(y), data = p, model = "within"))[1]),
    ab     = unname(coef(pgmm(y ~ lag(y, 1) | lag(y, 2:99), data = p,
                              effect = "individual", model = "onestep"))[1]))
}

round(rowMeans(replicate(200, sim())), 3)
```

With a true persistence of 0.6, pooled least squares returns roughly 0.92 and the within
estimator roughly 0.23. The Arellano-Bond estimator lands near 0.55, still a little low because
$T$ is short, but inside the bracket and close to the truth.

#### The Moment Conditions

@arellano1991some remove the firm effect by first differencing,

$$
\Delta y_{it} = \rho\, \Delta y_{i,t-1} + \Delta x_{it}'\beta + \Delta\varepsilon_{it},
$$

and then observe that if $\varepsilon_{it}$ is serially uncorrelated, levels of $y$ dated
$t-2$ and earlier are uncorrelated with $\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$ while remaining correlated with
$\Delta y_{i,t-1}$. That yields the moment conditions

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[y_{i,t-s}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\big] = 0, \qquad s \geq 2,
$$

one for every available lag at every period, which is where the instrument count comes from.
This is difference GMM.

@blundell1998initial point out that when the series is persistent, lagged levels are weak
instruments for differences: if $\rho$ approaches one, $\Delta y_{i,t-1}$ is nearly unpredictable
from past levels. They add a second block of moment conditions, using lagged differences as
instruments for the equation in levels, under the extra assumption that the initial condition is
uncorrelated with the firm effect. That is system GMM.

The two identifying assumptions are worth separating clearly. Difference GMM needs no serial
correlation in $\varepsilon_{it}$, which is testable in the sense that second-order serial
correlation in the differenced residuals would refute it. System GMM needs that plus a
restriction on the initial conditions, which is a statement about how the panel came to start
where it did and is not testable at all.

#### Replication: The Arellano-Bond Employment Equation

The original application is a panel of 140 UK firms observed from 1976 to 1984. It ships with
`plm`, so the published estimates can be reproduced directly.

```{r dynpanel-ab, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
data("EmplUK", package = "plm")

ab <- pgmm(log(emp) ~ lag(log(emp), 1:2) + lag(log(wage), 0:1) +
             log(capital) + lag(log(output), 0:1) | lag(log(emp), 2:99),
           data = EmplUK, effect = "twoways", model = "twosteps")

round(summary(ab, robust = FALSE)$coefficients[, 1:2], 3)
```

The coefficients reproduce the employment equation of @arellano1991some to three decimals:
0.474 on the first lag of employment, -0.053 on the second, -0.513 on the contemporaneous wage,
0.293 on capital. The standard errors printed here are the uncorrected two-step ones, which are
known to be severely downward biased in small samples; @windmeijer2005finite gives the finite
sample correction, and applied work should report corrected errors or one-step robust errors
instead.

The specification tests come with the estimator.

```{r dynpanel-ab-tests, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
s <- summary(ab, robust = FALSE)
c(n_instruments = length(ab$W[[1]][1, ]),
  n_firms       = length(ab$residuals),
  sargan_p      = round(s$sargan$p.value, 3),
  AR1_p         = round(s$m1$p.value, 3),
  AR2_p         = round(s$m2$p.value, 3))
```

Read them in the right order. First-order serial correlation in the differenced residuals is
expected and its presence is reassuring, not alarming, because differencing induces it
mechanically. Second-order correlation is the one that matters: rejecting it would say the
original errors were serially correlated and the lag structure is invalid. Here AR(1) rejects
and AR(2) does not, which is the pattern the design requires. The Sargan test does not reject.

#### The Result That Should Worry You

The estimator uses 38 instruments on 140 firms in the specification above. That ratio is already
high, and nothing stops it going higher, because the number of moment conditions grows with the
square of $T$. @roodman2009note showed what this does: with many instruments the weighting
matrix is estimated badly, the two-step standard errors collapse, and the overidentification test
loses all power, drifting toward a p-value of one.

The cheapest way to see the problem is to vary how deep the lag structure goes and watch the
estimate.

```{r dynpanel-instrument-count, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
depth <- function(L) {
  # pgmm parses the lag spec by non-standard evaluation, so the depth has to be
  # spliced into the formula as a literal rather than passed as a variable.
  fm <- as.formula(sprintf(paste(
    "log(emp) ~ lag(log(emp), 1:2) + lag(log(wage), 0:1) +",
    "log(capital) + lag(log(output), 0:1) | lag(log(emp), 2:%d)"), L))
  m <- pgmm(fm, data = EmplUK, effect = "twoways", model = "twosteps")
  data.frame(lags = paste0("2:", L),
             n_instruments = length(m$W[[1]][1, ]),
             rho_hat = round(unname(coef(m)[1]), 3),
             sargan_p = round(unname(summary(m, robust = FALSE)$sargan$p.value), 3))
}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(2, 3, 4, 99), depth))
```

The coefficient on lagged employment moves from -0.055 to 0.474 across these four
specifications. That is the whole range from "employment is not persistent at all" to
"employment is substantially persistent", and the only thing that changed is how many lags were
handed to the instrument matrix, a choice that is almost never reported and never pre-registered.
The Sargan test does not reject in any of the four. It is not adjudicating between them.

This is the same lesson as the overidentification discussion earlier in this chapter, in a
setting where it bites harder, because here the instruments are all functions of the same series
and are about as far from independent as instruments can be. A non-rejecting Sargan or Hansen
test in a dynamic panel is close to uninformative, and with enough instruments it is guaranteed.

Difference and system GMM also disagree on these data. Fitting the system estimator returns a
coefficient on lagged employment near 0.94 against the 0.47 from difference GMM, which is
exactly the pattern @blundell1998initial predict when the series is persistent enough that
lagged levels are weak instruments for differences. Whether that is the system estimator
correcting a weak-instrument bias or the extra initial-conditions assumption doing the work is
not something the data will settle.

#### Use in Applied Business Research

The method entered finance and management largely through @wintoki2012endogeneity, who argue
that the relation between board structure and firm performance is dynamic, that past performance
determines current governance, and that a dynamic panel GMM specification addresses the resulting
simultaneity without requiring an external instrument. The paper is worth reading as a model of
how to argue for the design, and the specification tests it reports are the ones to imitate.

What it also illustrates is how the method gets used downstream. Because the estimator needs no
instrument the researcher has to defend by name, it is easy to present as a technical fix rather
than as a set of substantive assumptions about dynamics and initial conditions. It is neither a
cure for omitted variables that are time varying nor a substitute for a design.

A minimum reporting standard, following @roodman2009howto:

1.  Report the number of instruments alongside the number of groups, and keep the former well
    below the latter. If the count exceeds the group count the results should be treated as
    uninterpretable.
2.  Collapse the instrument matrix or restrict the lag depth, and show that the estimate is
    stable across those choices rather than reporting one specification.
3.  Report AR(1) and AR(2) tests and say which one you need to reject and which you need not to.
4.  Use Windmeijer-corrected standard errors for two-step estimates, or report one-step robust
    errors.
5.  Do not present a non-rejecting Hansen test as evidence of validity, and be suspicious of a
    Hansen p-value near one, which is a symptom of instrument proliferation rather than a clean
    bill of health.
6.  State the initial-conditions assumption in words if you use system GMM, and say why it is
    plausible in your setting.
